verses.text: Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman.
Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband.
Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband.
The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.
Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.
But I speak this by permission, and not of commandment.
For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that.
I say therefore to the unmarried and widows, It is good for them if they abide even as I.
But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn.
And unto the married I command, yet not I, but the Lord, Let not the wife depart from her husband:
But and if she depart, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband: and let not the husband put away his wife.
But to the rest speak I, not the Lord: If any brother hath a wife that believeth not, and she be pleased to dwell with him, let him not put her away.
And the woman which hath an husband that believeth not, and if he be pleased to dwell with her, let her not leave him.
For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband: else were your children unclean; but now are they holy.
But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace.
For what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband? or how knowest thou, O man, whether thou shalt save thy wife?
But as God hath distributed to every man, as the Lord hath called every one, so let him walk. And so ordain I in all churches.
Is any man called being circumcised? let him not become uncircumcised. Is any called in uncircumcision? let him not be circumcised.
Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God.
Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called.
Art thou called being a servant? care not for it: but if thou mayest be made free, use it rather.
For he that is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord’s freeman: likewise also he that is called, being free, is Christ’s servant.
Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men.
Brethren, let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God.
Now concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord: yet I give my judgment, as one that hath obtained mercy of the Lord to be faithful.
I suppose therefore that this is good for the present distress, I say, that it is good for a man so to be.
Art thou bound unto a wife? seek not to be loosed. Art thou loosed from a wife? seek not a wife.
But and if thou marry, thou hast not sinned; and if a virgin marry, she hath not sinned. Nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh: but I spare you.
But this I say, brethren, the time is short: it remaineth, that both they that have wives be as though they had none;
And they that weep, as though they wept not; and they that rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and they that buy, as though they possessed not;
And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away.
But I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord:
But he that is married careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please his wife.

There is difference also between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit: but she that is married careth for the things of the world, how she may please her husband.
And this I speak for your own profit; not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction.
But if any man think that he behaveth himself uncomely toward his virgin, if she pass the flower of her age, and need so require, let him do what he will, he sinneth not: let them marry.
Nevertheless he that standeth stedfast in his heart, having no necessity, but hath power over his own will, and hath so decreed in his heart that he will keep his virgin, doeth well.
So then he that giveth her in marriage doeth well; but he that giveth her not in marriage doeth better.
The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth; but if her husband be dead, she is at liberty to be married to whom she will; only in the Lord.
But she is happier if she so abide, after my judgment: and I think also that I have the Spirit of God.

summary: The chapter turns a corner in the letter: Paul stops answering reports carried to him and begins answering a letter sent to him. "Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman." Whether that sentence is Paul's own conviction or a Corinthian slogan he is quoting back, he immediately hedges it with realism — "Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband" — and then states the mutual obligation of marriage in language that refuses to privilege the husband: "Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband. The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife." Abstinence within marriage is permitted only as a temporary, agreed devotion — "except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer" — lest "Satan tempt you not for your incontinency." Paul is careful to mark the status of his own words: "I speak this by permission, and not of commandment." He wishes "that all men were even as I myself," yet grants that "every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that," and tells the unmarried and widows that continence is good, "But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn." On divorce he speaks with the Lord's own authority — "unto the married I command, yet not I, but the Lord, Let not the wife depart from her husband" — and where separation happens the options are narrow: "let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband." Then he addresses a case the Lord's earthly teaching had not covered, marriage to a pagan: "to the rest speak I, not the Lord." The believing spouse is not to initiate a break, because "the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife" and the children "now are they holy"; but "if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace." From marriage Paul generalizes a rule of Christian contentment: "as God hath distributed to every man, as the Lord hath called every one, so let him walk." Circumcision and uncircumcision are alike "nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God"; the slave is "the Lord’s freeman" and the free man is "Christ’s servant," and both are told, "Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men" — though if freedom is available, "use it rather." Turning last to "virgins," he again flags his authority honestly — "I have no commandment of the Lord: yet I give my judgment, as one that hath obtained mercy of the Lord to be faithful" — and grounds his counsel in the pressure of the hour: "this is good for the present distress," "the time is short," "the fashion of this world passeth away." Hence the strange counsel to hold everything loosely, "that both they that have wives be as though they had none; And they that weep, as though they wept not... and they that buy, as though they possessed not." Marriage is never called sin — "if thou marry, thou hast not sinned; and if a virgin marry, she hath not sinned" — but it divides attention, since the unmarried "careth for the things that belong to the Lord" while the married "careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please his wife." Paul's stated aim is not restriction but freedom: "not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction." He closes with a comparative that has echoed through Christian history — "he that giveth her in marriage doeth well; but he that giveth her not in marriage doeth better" — and with a widow's liberty to remarry "to whom she will; only in the Lord," adding, "But she is happier if she so abide, after my judgment: and I think also that I have the Spirit of God."
takeaways: The chapter's account of the marriage bed is startlingly symmetrical. "Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband" is followed by the reciprocal claim that "The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife." In a world where a husband's authority over his wife's body was assumed and the reverse was unthinkable, Paul states the obligation twice and in both directions. Marriage here is not ownership but mutual self-donation, and the only sanctioned interruption of it is jointly agreed, temporary, and prayerful — "except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer" — with a return commanded so that neither is exposed by the other's absence.

Paul is unusually transparent about the weight of his own words, and the chapter should be read with that grading in view. Some things are the Lord's binding command — "I command, yet not I, but the Lord, Let not the wife depart from her husband." Some things are apostolic ruling on ground the Lord's earthly teaching had not addressed — "But to the rest speak I, not the Lord." Some things are counsel, not law — "I speak this by permission, and not of commandment," and "Now concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord: yet I give my judgment." Yet even his judgment is not offered as mere opinion, since he ends, "I think also that I have the Spirit of God." The distinction between what binds and what advises is drawn inside Scripture itself, not imposed on it from outside.

Continence is treated as a gift rather than an achievement, and its absence as a fact to be honestly reckoned with rather than shamed. "I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that." The counsel to the unmarried and widows is immediately qualified: "But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn." Paul neither flatters the celibate as spiritually superior by nature nor treats marriage as a concession made in disgrace; he twice insists "thou hast not sinned." The whole logic collapses if the gift is turned into a rule imposed on those who have not received it.

In the mixed marriage, holiness is presented as the stronger contagion. Ordinary intuition would say the believing spouse is compromised by the unbelieving one; Paul says the reverse — "the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband: else were your children unclean; but now are they holy." The believer therefore does not initiate the break. But this is a claim about the reach of grace, not a mandate to cling: "if the unbelieving depart, let him depart... but God hath called us to peace," tempered by the open question, "what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband?" Hope for the other's conversion is real but not guaranteed, and peace outranks a marriage the unbeliever has already abandoned.

Between the sections on marriage Paul plants a general rule of Christian vocation: "as God hath distributed to every man, as the Lord hath called every one, so let him walk. And so ordain I in all churches." Conversion does not require dismantling one's social situation, because in Christ the markers that seemed decisive are relativized — "Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God." The slave is already "the Lord’s freeman" and the free man already "Christ’s servant." This is not fatalism: "if thou mayest be made free, use it rather," and "Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men." Present circumstances are the place where discipleship is lived, not the thing discipleship must first fix.

The chapter's asceticism is eschatological rather than dualist. Paul does not disparage bodies, spouses, joy, grief, or property; he says their claim on us is time-limited, because "the time is short" and "the fashion of this world passeth away." Hence the deliberately strained counsel that "they that have wives be as though they had none; And they that weep, as though they wept not; and they that rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and they that buy, as though they possessed not." The stated purpose is positive and pastoral, "not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction." Undivided attention, not the rejection of created goods, is what "doeth better" is measuring.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 19:3-12 — What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder... there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake
crossRefs.why: This is the Lord's teaching Paul explicitly defers to when he says "I command, yet not I, but the Lord." The Gospel scene supplies both halves of 1 Corinthians 7 at once: an indissoluble bond rooted in creation, and a voluntary renunciation of marriage for the kingdom that only some can receive — "He that is able to receive it, let him receive it" — which matches Paul's "every man hath his proper gift of God."

crossRefs.label: Genesis 2:18-24 — It is not good that the man should be alone... and they shall be one flesh
crossRefs.why: Paul's opening "It is good for a man not to touch a woman" sits in deliberate tension with the creation verdict that aloneness is "not good," and his account of mutual bodily claim in verses 3-4 presupposes the one-flesh union. Reading the two together prevents the chapter from being taken as a general verdict against marriage rather than as counsel addressed to a particular moment.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 — ye are not your own... for ye are bought with a price
crossRefs.why: The immediately preceding chapter establishes the premise this one applies. "Ye are bought with a price" appears in both, first to argue that the body belongs to the Lord and not to fornication, then to argue that the redeemed are not to become "the servants of men." The bodily ethics of chapter 7 are the working out of a purchase already announced.

crossRefs.label: Romans 7:2-3 — the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth
crossRefs.why: Paul states the same rule of the marriage bond that closes this chapter — "The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth; but if her husband be dead, she is at liberty" — and there uses it as an analogy for the believer's death to the law. The parallel shows the death-bounded permanence of marriage was a settled premise in his thought, stable enough to carry an argument about something else.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 5:31-32 — they two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church
crossRefs.why: Where 1 Corinthians 7 treats marriage pastorally and under time pressure, this passage supplies the theological depth that keeps the counsel from reading as a mere concession: the union is a sign of Christ and the Church. Catholic tradition especially reads the "great mystery" as the ground of marriage's sacramental character and therefore of the indissolubility Paul assumes in verses 10-11.

crossRefs.label: 1 John 2:17 — And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever
crossRefs.why: The same eschatological logic underwrites Paul's "the fashion of this world passeth away" and his counsel to use the world "as not abusing it." Both texts relativize present attachments by the transience of the age rather than by any claim that created things are evil, which is the key to reading verses 29-31 without slipping into contempt for the world.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes verses 10-11 as decisive for the indissolubility of marriage: the command is explicitly the Lord's own — "not I, but the Lord" — and the only permitted outcomes of a separation are named, "let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband." Remarriage while the spouse lives is not among the options, and verse 39 confirms the bond runs to death: "The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth." A consummated marriage between two baptized persons is therefore held to be indissoluble by any human power, so that a civil divorce cannot dissolve it and a separation for grave cause leaves the parties still bound. Verse 15 is read narrowly rather than as a general escape clause: it addresses the case Paul flags as his own ruling and not the Lord's, a marriage contracted between two unbaptized persons where the unbelieving spouse departs after the other's conversion, and the declaration that a deserted spouse is "not under bondage in such cases" grounds a specific dissolution in favor of the faith rather than a broad permission to remarry after desertion.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read marriage as a covenant of the created order rather than a sacrament conferring an indissoluble bond, and they read verse 15 more broadly. If the deserted believer "is not under bondage," most conclude the marriage bond itself is broken by the desertion and remarriage is permitted, since being freed from a bond one may not act upon would be a hollow freedom, and since "God hath called us to peace" reads oddly as a summons to permanent limbo. Many add adultery as a second ground on the strength of the Gospel exception clause, producing the classic Reformation position that desertion and adultery may dissolve a marriage. Some also press Paul's own distinction the other way: because he marks verse 12 as "But to the rest speak I, not the Lord," they treat the mixed-marriage ruling as pastoral application rather than a narrowly defined category. Both traditions agree that Christ forbids divorce, that reconciliation is the goal, that the believer must never be the one to initiate the break, and that abandonment by an unbeliever is not a sin the deserted spouse must carry.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading finds in this chapter a genuine ordering of goods in which consecrated virginity or celibacy, freely embraced for the Lord, is objectively the higher state, without marriage being anything less than good. Paul's comparative is not accidental: "he that giveth her in marriage doeth well; but he that giveth her not in marriage doeth better," and of the widow, "she is happier if she so abide, after my judgment: and I think also that I have the Spirit of God." The reason given is not that marriage is defiling but that it divides attention — the unmarried "careth for the things that belong to the Lord," the married "careth for the things that are of the world" — with the goal being "that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction." This is read as the scriptural root of the counsel of consecrated celibacy, of religious vows, and of the Latin Church's discipline of a celibate clergy, understood as a discipline chosen in imitation of a state Paul commends, not as a claim that marriage is impure.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters typically read Paul's preference as conditional rather than as a permanent ranking of states. He himself anchors it in circumstance — "this is good for the present distress" and "the time is short" — and he frames continence as a distributed gift, "every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that," which makes it a calling rather than a rung. The Reformers pressed hard against mandatory clerical celibacy on exactly this text, arguing that "if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn" forbids imposing on an office a gift God has not given to everyone who holds it, and that vows binding the unwilling produce the very "snare" Paul says he does not wish to cast. They also note Paul's insistence that marrying is not sin. Both traditions affirm that singleness freely undertaken for undistracted service to the Lord is a real and honorable Christian vocation, that it is a gift and not a merit, and that marriage is good.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes verse 14 as evidence that grace works through households and not only through individual decision: "the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband: else were your children unclean; but now are they holy." The children of such a union are described as already holy, not as awaiting a holiness they must later procure by their own profession, which coheres with the pattern of whole households being received in the apostolic mission and supports the practice of baptizing infants into the Church's life. The sanctification of the unbelieving spouse is understood as a real relational consecration that keeps the marriage itself honorable and makes the believing spouse an instrument of possible conversion — "what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband?" — rather than a declaration that the unbeliever is already saved.

counterpoint.summary: Protestants divide over this verse along a fault line internal to their own tradition. Reformed and Presbyterian readers use it much as the Catholic reading does, as covenantal evidence that children of a believing parent stand within the covenant community and are properly baptized. Baptist and free-church readers answer that the verse proves too much if pressed: the unbelieving spouse is "sanctified" by exactly the same verb, and no one concludes that the unbeliever is thereby saved or should be baptized, so "holy" here must mean set apart or legitimate in relation to the believing household rather than regenerate. On that reading Paul's point is pastoral reassurance to a convert worried that a pagan marriage defiles her and her children, not a rule about who receives baptism. Both traditions agree that the verse ascribes a genuine sanctifying influence to the believing spouse and that it forbids treating a mixed marriage as unclean.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
